question: PFAS contamination and the protection of mothers

While the Committee for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC) of the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) continues to assess over 3 500 submissions received during the consultation on the proposed restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), new evidence continues to demonstrate the scale and persistence of PFAS contamination.

For instance, the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) recently detected PFAS in all breast milk samples analysed from 1 629 women. In 18 % of cases, concentrations exceeded the health-based guidance value, suggesting exposure levels that may negatively affect health. RIVM has warned that excessive PFAS exposure in infants may impair immune system function. 1.

Does the Commission recognise that each additional derogation from a PFAS restriction prolongs contamination of Europe’s water, soil and food chains, while imposing the costs of remediation and related health and environmental impacts on society rather than on polluters?

When considering derogations, will the Commission ensure that the costs associated with PFAS pollution and the resulting impacts, including any necessary remediation, are borne by polluters, in line with the ‘polluter pays’ principle and consistent with the approach reflected in the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive?
While the restriction process is ongoing, what further measures will the Commission take to protect pregnant women, infants and other vulnerable groups from continued PFAS exposure?
